title: Through the roof (Mark 2:1–12)
hook: four friends dig through a roof to lower a paralyzed man to Jesus

segments.voice: Yesterday: a man with leprosy knelt, and Jesus touched him. Your line was I am willing.

Capernaum again, and word is out that Jesus is home. The house fills. Then the doorway. Then the street outside. Up the lane come four men carrying a fifth on a mat. He can't walk. They've carried him all this way, and now there's a wall of backs between them and the one person they came for. The easy thing would be to stand at the edge of that crowd, sigh, and carry him home. Tomorrow, maybe. These four look up.
screen: `A HOUSE FULL TO THE DOOR.` → `FOUR MEN, ONE MAT.` → `THEY LOOK UP.`

segments.voice: A Galilean village roof was usually flat: wooden beams, branches laid across, and a thick layer of packed clay on top. So the four climb up and start digging; Mark's Greek word means digging out a hole. Picture it from inside. Jesus is teaching, and dirt starts falling on everyone's heads. A patch of light opens. Then a man on a mat comes down on ropes. In the King James Bible: "they uncovered the roof where he was: and when they had broken it up, they let down the bed wherein the sick of the palsy lay." Then a small phrase: "When Jesus saw their faith." Their faith, not only the man on the mat's. Mark notices the four on the roof, sweating, clay under their nails. Their stubbornness counted. And Jesus's first words surprise everyone: "Son, thy sins be forgiven thee." Some teachers of the law think, who can forgive sins but God alone? Jesus answers with a question: which is easier to say, your sins are forgiven, or get up and walk? Then he tells the man to pick up his mat and go home, and he does, out through the crowd that wouldn't let him in. Christians read this in more than one way. Some hear a claim about who Jesus is, since he speaks the forgiveness the scribes say belongs to God alone. Others hear it about friendship: someone can be carried to healing by other people's faith. The crowd's verdict is the last line: "We never saw it on this fashion." Nobody had.
screen: `A ROOF OF BEAMS AND PACKED CLAY.` · `WHEN JESUS SAW THEIR FAITH.` · `SINS FORGIVEN, THEN THE MAT.` · `WE NEVER SAW IT ON THIS FASHION.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who is stuck right now, sick, grieving, out of work, just flat, and the crowd between them and help: the forms, the waiting, the silence. Ask what digging would look like: a second phone call when the first went unanswered, showing up with food instead of offering, driving them, asking again. If you pray, carry them before God the way the four carried that mat, one corner each; if you don't, hold them in mind and choose your one stubborn thing.
Paralytic, the man on the mat, carried by four friends who dug through a roof when a crowd wouldn't let them in.
Your line: friends who dig through roofs. Four friends, one mat, one roof. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Christians pray for friends by name, and churches often keep prayer lists and send people to visit, cook for or drive those who are sick, a practice some connect with the four friends on the roof.

chat.says: Why did those four friends dig through a roof just to get their friend to Jesus?
options: The crowd blocked the door, so they dug; Jesus saw their faith, not only his.
They wanted to get ahead of everyone who had been waiting in line.
They'd heard Jesus would only heal people who came to him alone.
chat.meaning: When Jesus saw their faith: the four on the roof counted. Someone can be carried to healing by other people's faith.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'most of us would' and the stock 'the line most people miss'; narrator no longer asserts Jesus 'speaks forgiveness as only God does' (now attributed to the scribes' own question); unsourced outside-stair and roof-sleeping details cut.
Roof construction (beams, branches, packed clay) and the outside stair are typical descriptions of Galilean village houses; confirm the phrasing 'usually'.
Mark 2:4 Greek exoryxantes, 'having dug out'; Luke 5:19 has 'through the tiling'. Confirm the trapdoor floor.
Two readings given side by side (Jesus's authority to forgive; being carried by others' faith). Confirm fair.
Original: παραλυτικός, etymology 'loosened at the side' (para + lyō); confirm the note.
The word is the title's head per the outline ('Through the roof'); the trapdoor's first floor plays on the English idiom.
